beats.say: Above your head right now, about forty-five thousand catalogued objects are racing around the Earth. Most of them are junk.
Each one moves at several kilometres every second. And when two of them collide, they don't just break. They multiply.
Scientists have a name for where that leads. A chain reaction that could make low orbit too dangerous to use.
It's called Kessler syndrome. And the European Space Agency now says that even if we stopped launching today, the junk would keep growing.
So how did we fill the sky with wreckage? And can we still stop the cascade?
In 1978, a NASA scientist named Donald Kessler published a paper with his colleague Burton Cour-Palais.
They borrowed an idea from the asteroid belt. Rocks collide, shatter, and the pieces collide again.
Kessler asked a simple question. What happens when we put enough satellites in orbit for the same thing to start?
His answer was unsettling. Each collision makes fragments, and every fragment raises the odds of the next collision.
Over time, the wreckage would form a belt around the Earth. A belt that we made ourselves.
His model said it could begin forming within that century, and become a serious problem in the next one. That next century is ours.
To see why even a tiny fragment matters, you have to understand one thing about orbit. Speed.
To stay in low orbit, an object must move at about seven to eight kilometres per second. Slow down, and it falls.
The space station moves at about five miles every second. It circles the whole planet sixteen times a day.
Two objects in different orbits can meet at around ten kilometres per second. That's the average impact speed NASA uses for debris.
And impact energy grows with the square of speed. Double the speed, and you get four times the punch.
The European Space Agency says a one centimetre sphere hitting at that speed strikes with the energy of a hand grenade.
Even smaller things leave marks. In 2016, astronaut Tim Peake photographed a seven millimetre chip in a window of the station's Cupola.
It was gouged out by a tiny piece of debris, possibly a fleck of paint or a sliver of metal.
The window held, because it is quadruple glazed. And the station is the most heavily shielded spacecraft ever flown.
Most satellites have no armour like that. So now imagine something far bigger than a paint fleck. Imagine a whole satellite.
On the eleventh of January 2007, China fired a missile at one of its own old weather satellites, called Fengyun One C.
It orbited about eight hundred and sixty kilometres up. The interceptor hit, and the satellite turned into a cloud.
Within two months, more than twelve hundred pieces had been catalogued. Eventually the count passed three thousand.
It became the largest debris-making event on record. At that height, much of it will stay for decades, even centuries.
Two years later came something nobody planned.
On the tenth of February 2009, a working Iridium communications satellite met a dead Russian satellite, Cosmos 2251, high over northern Siberia.
They were seven hundred and ninety kilometres up, crossing at almost a right angle, at more than eleven kilometres per second.
Both were destroyed in an instant. It was the first known accidental collision between two whole satellites.
Together they left more than two thousand catalogued fragments. A dead satellite that nobody could steer had hit a live one.
Then, in November 2021, Russia fired a missile at Cosmos 1408, an old Soviet spy satellite nobody was using.
More than fifteen hundred trackable fragments spread through low orbit, in a cloud that crossed the space station's path.
All seven people on board climbed into their Dragon and Soyuz capsules, ready to flee, and waited there for about two hours.
They came through safely. But the sky around them was about to get much busier.
In 2025 alone, there were more than three hundred launches, carrying over four thousand new satellites.
That's about ten new satellites going up every single day.
By late October 2026, astronomer Jonathan McDowell counted about seventeen thousand working satellites in orbit.
More than eleven thousand of them belong to one internet megaconstellation, Starlink. Swarms like it fly in thin, crowded shells.
The European Space Agency says working satellites are packed most tightly between about four hundred and six hundred kilometres up.
Around them, it counts roughly forty-five thousand catalogued objects. Dead satellites, spent rocket stages, and fragments.
And that's only what we can track. Its models estimate fifty-four thousand objects bigger than ten centimetres.
Then about one point two million pieces between one and ten centimetres. And around a hundred and thirty million smaller than that.
The middle group is the nightmare. Too small to track and dodge, but big enough to wreck a satellite.
The space station has already swerved out of the way of debris more than forty times since 1999.
So what happens when dodging is no longer enough?
Here is how a cascade works. Start with one collision in a crowded shell.
It makes a cloud of fragments. Over time, they spread around the planet, crossing the paths of other satellites.
Each fragment is a new bullet. One of them hits another satellite, and that collision makes a new cloud.
Now there are two clouds, then four. The more debris is already up there, the faster the next crash comes.
The only natural cleaner is the thin upper air, which slowly drags things down. Below six hundred kilometres, that takes several years.
At eight hundred kilometres, it can take centuries. Above a thousand, a thousand years or more.
The agency's 2026 report warns that the expected number of objects and collisions in low orbit is skyrocketing, in a runaway effect.
And even if no new satellites were launched, it says the debris would keep growing.
What would that cost us? The polar weather satellites that feed our forecasts fly about eight hundred and twenty kilometres up.
That's the same band where Fengyun and Iridium broke apart.
Satellite internet, Earth imaging, climate monitoring and human spaceflight all depend on low orbit too.
Even the GPS satellites, about twenty thousand kilometres up, have to be launched through the junk below them.
That's the trap. Not a wall in the sky, but a minefield we would have to cross every time we leave.
So, can we still stop it?
The first fix is simple. Stop leaving dead satellites behind. In 2022, America's F C C ruled that satellites must come down within five years of their mission ending.
That replaced the old twenty-five year guideline. And the European Space Agency's Zero Debris approach aims to sharply limit new debris by 2030.
Some satellites now carry drag sails. Thin sheets unfold at the end of the mission, catch the thin air, and pull the craft down faster.
But rules can't clean up what is already there. The agency says active debris removal is now required to stop the growth.
In 2024, a Japanese spacecraft called ADRAS J crept up on an abandoned rocket stage, and got within fifteen metres of it.
Next, the agency's ClearSpace One mission plans to grab a dead satellite with four robotic arms and drag it down to burn up. Launch is planned for 2029.
Kessler gave us the warning nearly fifty years ago. His paper also said the belt could be delayed, if we acted early.
The sky isn't lost yet. But the clock he started is still ticking.
